cards.title: Polynomial-size arithmetic formulas for the determinant
cards.formal:
Do there exist positive integers \(K,C\) such that for every integer \(n\ge1\) there is an arithmetic formula \(F_n\) over \(\mathbb C\) satisfying
\[\operatorname{size}(F_n)\le K n^C,\qquad \llbracket F_n\rrbracket=\operatorname{Det}_n(X),\]
where \(\llbracket F_n\rrbracket\) is its output as a formal commutative polynomial and
\[\operatorname{Det}_n(X)=\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)\prod_{i=1}^{n}x_{i,\pi(i)}?\]
The formula is a binary expression tree with arbitrary complex constants and addition, subtraction and multiplication. Computations may use cancellations, but intermediate expressions cannot be shared. The same constants \(K,C\) must work for all dimensions.
cards.definitions:
Polynomial and parameters. The matrix \(X=(x_{ij})_{1\le i,j\le n}\) has \(n^2\) distinct commuting indeterminates as its entries. The positive integer \(n\) is the matrix dimension, not the number of variables. The set \(S_n\) consists of all permutations of \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Define \(\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)=(-1)^{\operatorname{inv}(\pi)}\), where \(\operatorname{inv}(\pi)\) counts pairs \(i<j\) with \(\pi(i)>\pi(j)\). All calculations take place in the polynomial ring \(\mathbb C[x_{11},\ldots,x_{nn}]\). In particular \(\operatorname{Det}_1=x_{11}\); no invertibility or numerical-entry promise is imposed.

Formula syntax and evaluation. A formula is a finite rooted binary tree with ordered children. A leaf is labelled by one input variable or one constant in \(\mathbb C\). Each internal node is labelled \(+\), \(-\) or \(\times\) and computes the corresponding operation on the two child polynomials; subtraction uses left child minus right child. The root’s polynomial is denoted \(\llbracket F\rrbracket\). Every node other than the root has exactly one parent. Repeated uses of an expression therefore require separate copies of its entire subtree. No powers, determinants, summations or other compound expressions are primitive gates: any such shorthand in a proposed family must expand to allowed binary nodes.

Size. Every node counts once, including each occurrence of a variable or constant. Equivalently, a leaf has size one and a node with children \(A,B\) has size \(1+\operatorname{size}(A)+\operatorname{size}(B)\). Distinct leaves carrying the same value count separately. Define
\[L_{\det}(n)=\min\{\operatorname{size}(F):\llbracket F\rrbracket=\operatorname{Det}_n\}.\]
The set is nonempty by the finite permutation expansion, so this positive-integer minimum exists. The question is whether \(L_{\det}(n)\) is bounded by one fixed polynomial in \(n\). Allowing real constants in a size bound rather than positive integer \(K,C\) would give the same polynomial-boundedness claim.

Constants and nonuniformity. Each constant leaf has unit size regardless of its magnitude, algebraic degree or description length. Constants and the tree may depend arbitrarily on \(n\), and complex constants need not be computable or rational. They cannot depend on the values later substituted for input variables. There is no algorithmic or efficiency requirement for generating the family, and no bit-cost bound on its representation: the resource is algebraic tree size. The field \(\mathbb C\) is fixed throughout; the target is not a simultaneous assertion for all fields.

Exact unrestricted computation. The equality at the root is an exact polynomial identity, coefficient by coefficient. Approximation of coefficients, a limit of formulas or correct evaluation only on a restricted input set does not meet it. Division, inverses, comparisons, branching, input-dependent constants and additional input variables are not allowed. There is no restriction on depth, homogeneity, signs or coefficient magnitudes. Intermediate polynomials may have powers or monomials absent from the determinant, provided they cancel in the final identity. A polynomial is multilinear if every variable has exponent at most one in every monomial. The output determinant is multilinear, but the formula is not required to be multilinear at intermediate nodes.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence claim or its negation. For a positive answer, prove the existence of allowed formula trees for every dimension, their exact determinant identity, and one common polynomial size bound. A uniform construction is welcome but is not required by this nonuniform target. Count all copied subtrees and constant occurrences.

A negative answer must prove
\[\forall K,C\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \exists n\ge1:\ L_{\det}(n)>K n^C.\]
It must cover arbitrary complex constants and all unrestricted intermediate computations permitted above. Equivalently, for every \(K,C,N\ge1\), there must be some \(n\ge N\) violating that polynomial bound; finitely many exceptional dimensions can always be absorbed into its constant. It is not necessary to prove that every sufficiently large dimension violates every given polynomial, a stronger eventual-growth claim.

A fixed-power lower bound, such as \(\Omega(n^3)\), leaves larger polynomial bounds possible. Lower bounds only for multilinear, homogeneous, symmetric, monotone, bounded-depth, bounded-coefficient or noncommutative computations do not refute the stated unrestricted commutative claim. An exact identity using a small circuit with shared intermediate results is not yet a small formula, and a large size for one particular determinant expansion is not a lower bound for all formulas. A proof conditional on an unresolved separation must keep that assumption explicit and does not settle this unconditional question.
cards.why: The canonical test of whether reusing intermediate expressions gives a superpolynomial advantage over arithmetic expression trees, even for an efficiently computable polynomial.

importance.reason: A fundamental separation inside algebraic computation, equivalent to the formula-versus-branching-program question through determinant completeness and linked to many explicit polynomial families.

progress.text: Berkowitz gives division-free polynomial-size, \(O(\log ^{2} n)\)-depth determinant circuits; unfolding yields quasipolynomial-size formulas.
Kalorkoti proves an unrestricted \(\Omega (n^{3})\) formula lower bound for an n by n determinant, also allowing division.
Raz establishes \(n^{\Omega (\log  n)}\) lower bounds for formulas that remain multilinear at every gate; the original ECCC report precedes the journal publication.
Chaugule and coauthors relate formula complexity of Schur polynomials and generalized Vandermonde determinants to the generic determinant.
Boyapati–Chillara–Vempati retain the \(n^{\Omega(\log n)}\) multilinear lower bound with \(\Theta(n\log^6 n)\) nonzero entries; ECCC in June, CCC publication on 23 July.
The updated factoring primer explicitly records that polynomial-size symbolic determinant formulas are still unknown, despite new formula-factoring results.

cards.status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The June 2026 factoring revision explicitly leaves polynomial-size symbolic determinant formulas unknown. The July CCC sparse-determinant theorem restricts intermediate computations to multilinear formulas, while other inspected 2026 separations impose symmetry or noncommutativity. No matching unrestricted complex-field resolution was found in the bounded primary-source search; full external proofs were not independently certified.

context_blocks.text: The determinant is computationally easy when an algorithm may save intermediate work and reuse it. A formula imposes a stricter discipline: each computed quantity has only one consumer. To use the same expression twice, the expression must be copied. This can turn a compact computation graph into a much larger tree. The problem asks whether the determinant has an alternative expression that avoids this potential blow-up.

The permutation expansion has \(n!\) summands, but this does not prove that every formula is large. A product of short sums may represent many expanded monomials. For example, the \(2\times2\) determinant is \(x_{11}x_{22}-x_{12}x_{21}\), represented by seven nodes in the stated model. The challenge is one size bound for all dimensions, not finding finite expressions for individual matrices. Numerical Gaussian elimination also does not directly answer the symbolic tree-size question: its usual implementation reuses intermediate entries, divides and chooses pivots.

Berkowitz’s division-free construction gives polynomial-size arithmetic circuits of depth \(O(\log ^{2} n)\). Unfolding a bounded-fan-in circuit of that depth into a tree gives a formula of size \(2^{O(\log ^{2} n)}=n^{O(\log  n)}\). This is quasipolynomial, already far below the permutation expansion, but still larger than a fixed power of n. A polynomial-size formula would close this remaining gap.

The determinant is complete for polynomial-size algebraic branching programs. Such a program is a directed acyclic graph with a source and sink; affine-linear edge labels are multiplied along paths and the path products are summed. The class \(\mathrm{VBP}_{\mathbb C}\) consists of polynomial families with polynomially many variables, polynomial degree and polynomial-size branching programs, while \(\mathrm{VF}_{\mathbb C}\) uses formula trees. Every formula has a polynomial-size branching program, and every such branching program has a polynomial-size determinant representation. Thus the existence claim here is equivalent to \(\mathrm{VF}_{\mathbb C}=\mathrm{VBP}_{\mathbb C}\).

The larger class \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}\) permits polynomial-size arithmetic circuits, where gates may have several consumers, while retaining polynomially many variables and polynomial degree. The June 2026 factoring primer records \(\mathrm{VF}_{\mathbb C}\subseteq\mathrm{VBP}_{\mathbb C}\subseteq\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}\) without a known strict containment. It includes recent closure results for factoring formulas and still expressly leaves small determinant formulas unresolved. A positive answer here would identify the first two classes; it would not alone identify either with \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}\).

An unrestricted lower bound is known, but it is only a fixed power. Kalorkoti proves \(\Omega (n^{3})\) formula size for the n by n determinant, even in a model allowing division. Here n is the matrix dimension; there are \(n^{2}\) independent variables. Thus the bound is cubic in dimension and only a power \(3/2\) in the number of variables. It must not be described as a cubic lower bound in the input-variable count.

Raz proves a much stronger \(n^{\Omega (\log  n)}\) lower bound when every intermediate polynomial is multilinear. This restriction is substantive even though the final determinant is multilinear. For a simple illustration, \((x+y)^{2}- x^{2}- y^{2}\) equals 2xy, a multilinear output obtained through nonmultilinear intermediate terms. The example does not establish a size advantage, but it shows why output multilinearity alone cannot justify applying a theorem that assumes multilinearity throughout a computation.

Recent progress tests which determinant features are needed for that restricted lower bound. Boyapati, Chillara and Vempati prove the existence of sparse n by n symbolic matrices with only \(\Theta (n \log ^{6} n)\) nonzero entries whose determinants still require \(n^{\Omega (\log  n)}\) multilinear formulas. This shows that the dense \(n^{2}\)-variable presentation is not essential to Raz’s obstruction. It leaves the permission to use nonmultilinear intermediate computations untouched.

The question also organizes complexity outside generic matrices. Chaugule and coauthors connect small formulas for Schur polynomials and generalized Vandermonde determinants to small formulas for the general determinant. Such reductions make the determinant a useful benchmark for whether apparently special algebraic expressions really admit efficient tree computations. A separation would reveal a basic cost of forbidding reuse, already within problems that possess efficient arithmetic circuits.

sentences: The symbolic determinant has n² commuting input variables for an n-by-n matrix.
The question asks whether its exact polynomial can be expressed by arithmetic trees of size bounded by one fixed polynomial in n.
Every occurrence of a variable, constant or copied subexpression is charged, while arbitrary fixed complex constants and cancellations are allowed.
A complete Lean proof must establish such formulas for all dimensions or refute every polynomial size bound in the full nonuniform model.
Cubic unrestricted lower bounds and superpolynomial multilinear lower bounds do not settle this equivalent formulation of VF versus VBP over the complex field.

source_formulation.text: The inherited Raz source treats general arithmetic formulas over fields and separately proves a multilinear lower bound. This card retains the previously chosen complex-field specialization, nonuniform arbitrary constants, binary operations, total-node size, polynomial-existence target and importance 96. The review makes evaluation and size recursive, spells out the exact quantifier negation, and does not import intermediate multilinearity or symmetry from restricted lower-bound results.

Checked official CCC 2026.33 metadata: LIPIcs 383, 33:1–33:21, 23 July publication, distinct from May submission and June ECCC posting.

Read factoring primer TR25-083 revision 1 (12 June 2026), §7.1, Definition 7.2, Remark 7.3 and pp.53–54: VF subset VBP subset VP, no known strict containment, symbolic determinant formulas still unknown despite the 2025 factor-closure breakthrough.

Bounded later searches through 16 September 2026 screened arXiv:2601.09343 symmetry/orbit-size separations and the 30 July TR26-061 revision on noncommutative circuit lower bounds; read their primary abstracts. These are different restrictions/operations. TR26-043 concerns a barrier for the min-partition-rank method on multilinear ABPs, not an unrestricted determinant formula theorem. No matching general resolution was found.

Checked arbitrary-complex-constant quantifiers, ordered subtraction nodes, copied-subtree cost, exact versus limiting computation, finite minimum-size existence and the exact negation. Related active TCS-6611 and TCS-6612 retain their distinct permanent/representation and VP/VBP targets. No archive body was read; external proofs were not independently formalized.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Inactive records are archived outside the catalogue, exports and editorial work. Their content, stable IDs and reasons are retained; imports cannot reactivate them. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Inactive cards, including resolved records, are archived outside the ranking without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
